research.title: The Root Hypothesis
research.question: Can surviving traditions be traced toward one earlier common religious or cosmological tradition?

sections.title: What would count as common ancestry?
sections.body: A common ancestor is a model to test. It would need a dated chain of evidence and a set of distinctive shared features. Water, darkness or divine beings alone are too general to decide among competing models.

sections.title: Evidence for common ancestry
sections.body: No global common ancestor is established by this initial corpus. The project has not yet assembled the linguistic, archaeological and chronological evidence needed to evaluate that proposition. This is a research status, not a disproof.

sections.title: Evidence for borrowing
sections.body: The Kumarbi–Hesiod comparison offers a specific research lead involving divine succession and genital violence. The current relationship record is disputed, with moderate confidence in the relevance of comparison. It does not assert direct textual dependence.

sections.title: Independent development
sections.body: Test whether ordinary human experiences, environments and political institutions could account for broad patterns. Similarity does not rule out independent development; difference does not establish it.

sections.title: Chronology problems
sections.body: Composition, oral precursors, earliest attestation and dates of surviving copies must be modeled separately. The Shabaka Stone’s claim to preserve old writing is itself evidence to examine, not a surviving ancient original.

sections.title: Geographical problems
sections.body: Ugarit’s dated contact with the Hittite kingdom provides one investigated contact edge. Contact allows a possible route; it does not demonstrate movement of any particular myth. No global genealogical tree is drawn.

sections.title: Linguistic evidence
sections.body: TODO: compare original words, productive roots, borrowing phonology and semantic range. A translated word such as “chaos” or “staff” is not a linguistic cognate.

sections.title: Archaeological evidence
sections.body: Objects can supply physical dates and contexts. The Egyptian ivory wand has a material history; a literary staff has a narrative history. These are different kinds of records, requiring different tests.

sections.title: Missing evidence
sections.body: Unattested oral traditions, lost manuscripts, uncertain composition dates and uneven excavation leave substantial gaps. A missing link is a research gap; it cannot be filled by drawing an arrow.

sections.title: Competing models
sections.body: Keep five models open: local continuity; borrowing through contact; shared regional inheritance; independent development; a much earlier common source. They need not be mutually exclusive at every scale. For each proposed connection, record what discovery could weaken or strengthen it.

next_steps: Build a passage-specific chronology and a dated contact register.
Compare distinctive clusters without counting several retellings of one source as independent evidence.
Commission philological and archaeological review before assigning high-confidence ancestry.

research.title: Staff, rod & scepter
research.question: Which similarities survive when we compare the original terms and the objects’ actual roles?

sections.title: Start with the word
sections.body: Moses’ and Aaron’s implements are called maṭṭeh in the selected Hebrew passages. Hesiod’s gift is a skēptron. The English overlap does not establish that they are the same kind of object.

sections.title: Keep the extraordinary claim
sections.body: Exodus describes transformations and a staff swallowing rival staffs. Hesiod describes the Muses giving him a staff and voice. Record those claims without replacing them with symbolism or treating them as demonstrated physical events.

sections.title: Who acts?
sections.body: The object records distinguish wielder, attributed powers and source of power. Hesiod’s divine voice is given by the Muses; the passage does not attribute an autonomous mechanism to the wood.

sections.title: A physical comparison
sections.body: Met 86.1.91 is a curved ivory implement with protective figures. Its association with infant protection and rebirth is the museum’s interpretation; the catalogue title “Magic Wand” does not supply an ancient Egyptian word.

sections.title: What remains unproved
sections.body: No cross-cultural identity, identical power source or common origin for these objects is established here. Comparables are research leads, currently speculative.

next_steps: Verify original Egyptian names for each object type.
Add royal scepters, Mesopotamian rods and rings, Hermes’ staff and healing serpent iconography as separate dossiers.
Establish earliest attestations from a witness census; do not use the oldest item currently entered as the earliest known.

research.title: Creation from a primordial state
research.question: What existed first, and what does each text say changes?

sections.title: Compare passages of comparable scope
sections.body: Genesis 1 describes darkness, deep and waters. Enuma Elish begins with Apsu and Tiamat’s mingled waters. Hesiod places Chaos first. These are three differently worded beginnings.

sections.title: Respect fragments and composite traditions
sections.body: The Sumerian flood story opens after a large lacuna. The modern Hermopolitan dossier draws on references such as CT 76, not a surviving continuous epic.

sections.title: Creation and sovereignty
sections.body: Baal’s victory over Yam should not be silently turned into a full account of world creation. The interpretation of divine combat as creation is a scholarly question.

next_steps: Collate Egyptian primary passages and the remaining Enuma Elish tablets.
Record several scholarly positions on chaos terminology and Genesis composition.

research.title: The making of humanity
research.question: Which materials, actions and purposes are actually named?

sections.title: Three materials, distinct descriptions
sections.body: Genesis 2:7 specifies ground-dust and the breath of life. Atrahasis’s creation passage mixes clay with divine flesh and blood. Enuma Elish VI names Qingu’s blood and the transfer of divine work to humanity.

sections.title: Do not turn a tag into a translation
sections.body: “Humanity from earth” and “humanity from clay” remain distinct motifs. Material similarity is relevant, but a claim of borrowing requires additional evidence.

sections.title: The scope of Hesiod’s account
sections.body: The Theogony describes the fashioning of the first woman in Zeus’s response to Prometheus. It does not provide a symmetric origin account for all humans in this passage.

next_steps: Add Enki and Ninmah with original Sumerian terminology.
Separate the formation of bodies, animation, social function and mortality.

research.title: Flood & survival
research.question: What is preserved about destruction, survivors and the aftermath?

sections.title: Sumerian survival
sections.body: The Sumerian flood story describes a boat enduring seven days and nights, the return of the sun, sacrifice and Ziusudra’s exceptional life. Its missing stretches must remain visible.

sections.title: The next controlled comparison
sections.body: Atrahasis has a flood tradition, represented here by catalogued tablets, but the full episode still needs passage-level collation. Genesis 6–9 and Gilgamesh XI are queued expansions. A complete flood comparison is not claimed.

sections.title: Historical event questions
sections.body: A literary flood report and archaeological flood deposits answer different questions. Connecting them requires independent dating, regional evidence and criteria for distinguishing ordinary flooding from a specific claimed event.

next_steps: Collate Genesis 6–9, Atrahasis III and Gilgamesh XI.
Keep boat shape, duration, animal preservation and landing-place claims tied to their individual versions.

research.title: Divine generations & succession
research.question: Does a shared sequence indicate transmission or only a comparable pattern?

sections.title: The paired passages
sections.body: In Hesiod, Kronos attacks Ouranos with a sickle. In the Hittite-Hurrian material summarized by Powell, Kumarbi bites off Anu’s genitals. The distinctive resemblance motivates investigation; the mechanisms differ.

sections.title: A testable relationship
sections.body: Keep contact, chronology, literary sequence and differences in separate fields. Do not equate a storm god with every other storm god or infer direct dependence from the name of a motif.

next_steps: Replace the Kumarbi summary with a collated primary dossier.
Add Ullikummi without merging its plot into the Song of Emergence.

research.title: Serpents in context
research.question: When is a serpent a speaking character, transformed object, image or modern interpretation?

sections.title: Keep the roles separate
sections.body: Genesis 3 presents a speaking serpent. Exodus 4 describes a staff becoming a serpent. Exodus 7 uses a different Hebrew creature term, tannîn, in the Aaron episode. Similar English renderings should not erase these differences.

sections.title: Interpretations are additional evidence
sections.body: Later identifications and healing symbolism require their own dated texts or objects. This dossier does not project them into the creation narrative.

next_steps: Add original-language lexical references for nāḥāš and tannîn.
